title: The words behind digital experience, without the jargon
introduction: Content management, portals and experience platforms: the vocabulary digital teams use every day, explained so it lands the first time.
explanation: Each entry defines a term, then explains how it differs from a related concept. Follow the linked Jahia resources to explore examples, use cases and practical guidance.

entries.title: B2B customer portal
entries.summary: An authenticated space where a business customer finds its contracts, orders and support history in one place.
entries.body: An authenticated space where a business customer finds its contracts, orders and support history in one place.
entries.comparisonTitle: B2B customer portal vs e-commerce website
entries.comparison: An e-commerce website centers on buying. A B2B customer portal also supports the ongoing account relationship: contracts, service requests and documents governed by customer permissions.

entries.title: Cloud content management
entries.summary: Content management whose infrastructure is run by a provider rather than hosted and patched in house.
entries.body: Content management whose infrastructure is run by a provider rather than hosted and patched in house.
entries.comparisonTitle: Cloud content management vs headless CMS
entries.comparison: Cloud describes where the system runs and who operates it. Headless describes how content reaches an interface. A cloud CMS can be traditional, headless or hybrid.

entries.title: CMS migration
entries.summary: Moving from one content management system to another: content, templates, redirects and rankings.
entries.body: Moving from one content management system to another: content, templates, redirects and rankings.
entries.comparison: A redesign changes presentation and journeys. A CMS migration changes the system that stores and delivers content. The two can happen together, but migration also requires content mapping, URL redirects and editorial checks.

entries.title: Composable DXP vs monolithic
entries.summary: Assembling chosen components against buying one integrated suite, and the criterion that actually decides it.
entries.body: Assembling chosen components against buying one integrated suite, and the criterion that actually decides it.
entries.comparison: Composable describes how capabilities are assembled across products. Headless describes separation between content delivery and presentation. A headless CMS can be one part of a composable architecture; it does not make every integration composable.

entries.title: Content as a service
entries.summary: Content exposed through an API and consumed by any interface, with no page defined in advance.
entries.body: Content exposed through an API and consumed by any interface, with no page defined in advance.
entries.comparisonTitle: Content as a service vs software as a service
entries.comparison: Content as a service describes delivering content through APIs. Software as a service describes how software is operated and purchased. The first concerns content delivery; the second concerns the operating model.

entries.title: Content lifecycle
entries.summary: The stages a piece of content goes through from creation to archiving, and who answers for each one.
entries.body: The stages a piece of content goes through from creation to archiving, and who answers for each one.
entries.comparison: The lifecycle covers the whole life of content, including review, retirement and archiving. A workflow specifies the tasks, roles and approvals used during particular stages.

entries.title: Content management system
entries.summary: The system that stores, organises and publishes a site's content without going through code.
entries.body: The system that stores, organises and publishes a site's content without going through code.
entries.comparison: A CMS manages and publishes content. A DXP coordinates a broader set of experience capabilities, which can include personalization, integrations and analytics alongside content management. The scope matters more than the product label.

entries.title: Content workflow
entries.summary: The path a piece of content travels between drafting and publication, and who approves what along it.
entries.body: The path a piece of content travels between drafting and publication, and who approves what along it.
entries.comparison: Approval is a decision within a workflow. The workflow also defines assignment, review, translation, scheduled publication and what happens when a change is rejected.

entries.title: DAM vs CMS
entries.summary: Managing media files against managing pages, and why one does not replace the other.
entries.body: Managing media files against managing pages, and why one does not replace the other.
entries.comparisonTitle: DAM vs CMS: assets and experiences
entries.comparison: A DAM organizes reusable media, metadata and usage rights. A CMS organizes editorial content and its publication. They can work together: an approved asset in the DAM can appear in several CMS pages.

entries.title: Digital asset management
entries.summary: The system that centralises images, video and documents with their metadata and usage rights.
entries.body: The system that centralises images, video and documents with their metadata and usage rights.
entries.comparisonTitle: Digital asset management vs file storage
entries.comparison: File storage holds files. DAM adds asset-specific organization and governance, such as metadata, renditions and usage rights. The useful distinction is how assets are found, approved and reused.

entries.title: Digital experience platform
entries.summary: A platform that brings content management, customer data and personalisation onto one foundation.
entries.body: A platform that brings content management, customer data and personalisation onto one foundation.
entries.comparisonTitle: DXP vs a collection of tools
entries.comparison: A set of tools becomes a coordinated experience platform through shared integrations, governance and delivery processes. Buying several products alone does not connect customer journeys or content.

entries.title: DXP vs CMS
entries.summary: Where a content management system stops and an experience platform begins.
entries.body: Where a content management system stops and an experience platform begins.
entries.comparisonTitle: DXP vs CMS: broader scope, not a replacement rule
entries.comparison: A CMS can be the content foundation of a DXP. The distinction is the scope of the experience being managed, rather than a rule that every organization must replace its CMS with a larger suite.

entries.title: Enterprise CMS
entries.summary: A content management system built for multisite, multilingual and the governance large teams need.
entries.body: A content management system built for multisite, multilingual and the governance large teams need.
entries.comparisonTitle: Enterprise CMS vs a large website
entries.comparison: Enterprise describes requirements such as permissions, governance, integrations and operations across teams. Page count alone does not determine whether a CMS meets those requirements.

entries.title: Extranet
entries.summary: An authenticated space opened to third parties: partners, suppliers, resellers or customers.
entries.body: An authenticated space opened to third parties: partners, suppliers, resellers or customers.
entries.comparison: An intranet serves employees. An extranet gives approved external users access to selected services or information. Both may require authentication; the audience and access boundaries distinguish them.

entries.title: Headless CMS
entries.summary: A content management system with no presentation layer, delivering content to any front end through an API.
entries.body: A content management system with no presentation layer, delivering content to any front end through an API.
entries.comparison: A headless CMS delivers content through APIs and leaves interface rendering to another application. A traditional CMS also supplies the presentation layer. Headless therefore changes who owns delivery, previews and front-end development.

entries.title: Headless CMS vs DAM
entries.summary: Structured content on one side, media files on the other: two jobs rarely given to the same tool.
entries.body: Structured content on one side, media files on the other: two jobs rarely given to the same tool.
entries.comparisonTitle: Headless CMS vs DAM: structured content and media
entries.comparison: A headless CMS manages structured editorial content for applications. A DAM manages reusable digital assets and their metadata. An API does not make the two systems interchangeable.

entries.title: Headless vs decoupled vs hybrid
entries.summary: Three architectures the market confuses constantly, and the one criterion that separates them.
entries.body: Three architectures the market confuses constantly, and the one criterion that separates them.
entries.comparisonTitle: Headless, decoupled and hybrid: check capabilities
entries.comparison: Headless removes the built-in presentation layer. Decoupled separates authoring from delivery while a delivery layer may still be supplied. Hybrid combines page-oriented and API delivery. Vendor terminology varies, so verify preview and authoring capabilities.

entries.title: Headless vs traditional CMS
entries.summary: Delivering through an API against publishing with built-in templates, and what each one costs.
entries.body: Delivering through an API against publishing with built-in templates, and what each one costs.
entries.comparison: Traditional systems include a website rendering approach. Headless systems expose content for a separately built interface. Compare editorial preview, development ownership and channel needs before choosing either model.

entries.title: Hybrid CMS
entries.summary: A system that serves both templated pages and an API, so the choice does not have to be made once and for all.
entries.body: A system that serves both templated pages and an API, so the choice does not have to be made once and for all.
entries.comparison: A hybrid CMS supports both page-based authoring and API delivery. A purely headless CMS delegates presentation to external applications. Hybrid does not mean every channel automatically shares the same layout.

entries.title: Intranet
entries.summary: An authenticated space built for the people who work at an organisation.
entries.body: An authenticated space built for the people who work at an organisation.
entries.comparison: An intranet is the internal digital environment for employees. An employee portal is an entry point to services and information within that environment. The terms overlap, but a portal need not encompass the whole intranet.

entries.title: Intranet vs extranet
entries.summary: The same mechanism, two opposite audiences, and the confusion that costs the most at scoping.
entries.body: The same mechanism, two opposite audiences, and the confusion that costs the most at scoping.
entries.comparisonTitle: Intranet vs extranet: audience, not technology
entries.comparison: An intranet serves internal users; an extranet serves authorized external users. They may use the same platform, but require distinct access policies, content ownership and user journeys.

entries.title: Multilingual CMS
entries.summary: A system that runs several languages inside one site without duplicating content or structure.
entries.body: A system that runs several languages inside one site without duplicating content or structure.
entries.comparison: A multilingual CMS manages language versions and their publication. Automatic translation produces a draft translation. Editorial review, regional adaptation and language-specific URLs remain separate responsibilities.

entries.title: Multisite CMS
entries.summary: A system that runs several sites from one instance, with shared content and shared design.
entries.body: A system that runs several sites from one instance, with shared content and shared design.
entries.comparison: Multisite manages several sites with shared or delegated governance. Multilingual manages several language versions. A single site can be multilingual, and a multisite estate can use just one language.

entries.title: On-premise vs cloud hosting
entries.summary: Hosting it yourself or having it hosted, and what each choice changes for control, cost and compliance.
entries.body: Hosting it yourself or having it hosted, and what each choice changes for control, cost and compliance.
entries.comparison: On-premise and cloud describe deployment and operational responsibility. They do not decide whether a CMS is headless or traditional. Compare data location, maintenance ownership and service commitments separately.

entries.title: Open source vs proprietary CMS
entries.summary: Open code against a closed licence: what each implies for governance, cost and the exit route.
entries.body: Open code against a closed licence: what each implies for governance, cost and the exit route.
entries.comparisonTitle: Open source vs free software pricing
entries.comparison: Open source concerns license rights to inspect, use and modify source code. It does not remove hosting, support or maintenance costs. Proprietary and open-source products both need an operating and support budget.

entries.title: Self-service portal
entries.summary: A portal whose job is to let someone finish a task without reaching a person.
entries.body: A portal whose job is to let someone finish a task without reaching a person.
entries.comparison: A knowledge base helps users find answers. A self-service portal also lets them complete tasks, such as updating details or tracking a request. A knowledge base can be one service inside the portal.

entries.title: Site search
entries.summary: The engine that indexes and queries a site's or a portal's content, including what sits behind a login.
entries.body: The engine that indexes and queries a site's or a portal's content, including what sits behind a login.
entries.comparison: Site search retrieves content from a defined site or connected content sources. Web search retrieves pages across the public web. Site search must also account for the permissions and vocabulary of its own audience.

entries.title: Static vs dynamic website
entries.summary: Pages built in advance against pages built on request: speed, freshness and what it costs to run.
entries.body: Pages built in advance against pages built on request: speed, freshness and what it costs to run.
entries.comparison: Static and dynamic describe how a response is generated. Interactivity describes behavior in the browser. A statically generated page can be interactive, while a dynamically generated page may contain no interactive controls.

entries.title: Types of web portals
entries.summary: The full typology of portals, by audience and by function, and what actually tells them apart.
entries.body: The full typology of portals, by audience and by function, and what actually tells them apart.
entries.comparison: Customer, partner and employee portals describe audiences and tasks. CMS, DXP and custom applications describe implementation approaches. Choose the portal audience first, then assess the capabilities needed to serve it.

entries.title: Web portal
entries.summary: A single entry point that assembles content, services and personalised data behind one authentication.
entries.body: A single entry point that assembles content, services and personalised data behind one authentication.
entries.comparison: A portal is a type of website that brings services and information together for a defined audience. Its distinguishing purpose is helping users access relevant services, often using roles and permissions. A public website primarily presenting information does not necessarily provide those workflows.
